pharm: Functionalized amino acid; selectively enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels
quick: Monotherapy 100 mg BID start, maint 150-200 mg BID; adjunctive 50 mg BID start (max 200 mg BID)
Animal data suggest fetal harm; enroll in NAAED registry

Mild-moderate: reduce max dose 25%; severe not recommended
summary: Lacosamide is a functionalized amino-acid antiepileptic that selectively enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels. It is indicated for partial-onset seizures (monotherapy or adjunctive) and as adjunctive therapy for primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures in patients 4 years and older, with oral and intravenous formulations that are dosed equivalently. It is a Schedule V controlled substance, prolongs the PR interval, and requires gradual titration. Watch for suicidal ideation, dizziness/ataxia, cardiac conduction effects, and syncope, and taper to discontinue.
indications: Treatment of partial-onset seizures in patients 4 years of age and older (monotherapy or adjunctive therapy)
Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures in patients 4 years of age and older

admin: May be taken with or without food; oral and intravenous doses are the same
Titrate gradually, no more frequently than once per week
A single loading dose of 200 mg approximates steady state of 100 mg twice daily where rapid onset is needed
IV is for use only when oral administration is temporarily not feasible; infuse over 15 to 60 minutes
Obtain an ECG before starting and after titration to steady state in patients with proarrhythmic conditions or on conduction-affecting drugs
Withdraw gradually (over at least 1 week) to minimize risk of increased seizure frequency
moa: The precise antiepileptic mechanism is not fully elucidated. In vitro electrophysiological studies show lacosamide selectively enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels, stabilizing hyperexcitable neuronal membranes and inhibiting repetitive neuronal firing.

relative: Underlying proarrhythmic conditions (e.g., known conduction problems, severe cardiac disease)
Concomitant medications that affect cardiac conduction (sodium/beta/calcium/potassium channel blockers, PR-prolonging drugs)
Concurrent strong CYP3A4/CYP2C9 inhibitors in renal or hepatic impairment
monitor: Suicidal thoughts and behavior, depression, mood/behavior changes
ECG and PR interval in at-risk patients before and after titration

preg: Based on animal data, lacosamide may cause fetal harm; rats showed increased embryofetal and perinatal mortality, growth deficit, and developmental neurotoxicity at clinically relevant exposures. Available human data from the NAAED registry, a cohort study, and case reports are insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. Encourage enrollment in the North American Antiepileptic Drug (NAAED) pregnancy registry (1-888-233-2334).
renal: Lacosamide and its major metabolite are eliminated primarily by renal excretion. No dosage adjustment is needed for mild to moderate impairment; AUC rose ~25% in mild/moderate and ~60% in severe impairment. For severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) or end-stage renal disease, reduce the maximum dosage by 25%. Lacosamide is effectively removed by hemodialysis (AUC reduced ~50% after 4 hours); consider dosage supplementation of up to 50% after dialysis. Initiate and titrate based on clinical response and tolerability.
hepatic: Moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B) increases lacosamide AUC by approximately 50-60%. For mild or moderate hepatic impairment, reduce the maximum dosage by 25%. Pharmacokinetics have not been evaluated in severe hepatic impairment and use is not recommended.

major: Drugs affecting cardiac conduction (sodium/beta/calcium/potassium channel blockers, PR-prolonging AEDs) - risk of AV block, bradycardia, or ventricular tachyarrhythmia; obtain ECG and monitor closely
Other CNS depressants and alcohol - additive dizziness, sedation, and CNS depression
moderate: Strong CYP3A4 or CYP2C9 inhibitors in renal or hepatic impairment - significantly increased lacosamide exposure; dose reduction may be necessary
interactions.food: Food does not affect the rate or extent of absorption; may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive CNS depression, dizziness, and ataxia.
interactions.diagnostics: Reversible elevations in liver function tests (ALT) have occurred; monitor as clinically indicated.

serious: Cardiac rhythm and conduction abnormalities (PR prolongation, AV block, bradycardia)
Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)/multi-organ hypersensitivity
Increased seizure frequency on abrupt withdrawal
emergency: Second- or third-degree AV block, severe bradycardia, or syncope
DRESS/multi-organ hypersensitivity (rash with fever, eosinophilia, organ involvement)

monitoring: Emergence or worsening of depression, suicidal thoughts or behavior, and mood/behavior changes
ECG before initiation and after titration to steady state in patients with proarrhythmic conditions or conduction-affecting drugs
Dizziness, ataxia, and syncope, especially during titration and with IV use
Signs of DRESS/hypersensitivity and liver function tests
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed; do not stop suddenly - the dose must be tapered to avoid more seizures
Watch for and report any new or worsening depression or thoughts of suicide
May cause dizziness, double vision, or fainting; avoid driving or hazardous tasks until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol, which can worsen dizziness and drowsiness
Report a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, or fainting spells
Seek care for rash with fever, swollen glands, or facial swelling (possible serious hypersensitivity)
Tell your clinician if pregnant or planning pregnancy and consider enrolling in the AED pregnancy registry
This is a controlled medicine (Schedule V); store securely
pk: Completely absorbed orally; bioavailability ~100%, negligible first-pass effect
Peak plasma concentration approximately 1 to 4 hours after oral dosing
Approximately 13 hours (unchanged drug); steady state in ~3 days
Dosed twice daily; metabolized by CYP3A4/CYP2C9/CYP2C19 and renal excretion
Injection: store at 20-25C (68-77F), excursions 15-30C; do not freeze; discard unused portion
pearls: Schedule V controlled substance; high doses produced euphoria-type responses in abuse studies
Causes a small, dose-related increase in PR interval but does not prolong QTc
Oral and IV doses are identical (bioavailability ~100%); a 200 mg loading dose mimics 100 mg BID steady state
Effectively dialyzable - consider up to 50% supplemental dose after hemodialysis
Reduce maximum dose by 25% in severe renal impairment/ESRD and in mild-moderate hepatic impairment; avoid in severe hepatic impairment
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose and resume the regular twice-daily schedule. Do not take a double dose. Do not stop lacosamide or change the schedule without medical advice, because abruptly stopping can increase seizures.
overdose: Reported effects after intake of more than 800 mg (twice the maximum recommended daily dose) include dizziness, nausea, and seizures (generalized tonic-clonic, status epilepticus); cardiac conduction disorders, confusion, decreased consciousness, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, and coma have also occurred, and fatalities have followed overdoses of several grams. There is no specific antidote. Provide standard decontamination and general supportive care with monitoring of vital signs and clinical status, and contact a Certified Poison Control Center. Standard hemodialysis significantly clears lacosamide (systemic exposure reduced ~50% in 4 hours) and may be indicated based on clinical state or significant renal impairment.
